title: A Bell Test on Where Atoms Are Going
hook: Bell's inequality has fallen for photons and atomic spins. Now for motion itself — entangled helium atoms that defy local realism about their own momentum.
key_points: Bell's theorem says no local-realist theory can reproduce all of quantum mechanics' correlations.
Previous violations used photons or the internal states of massive particles — never their motional states.
This experiment entangles the momenta of pairs of metastable helium atoms and reads them out with matter-wave interferometry.
The measured CHSH parameter is S = 2.52 +/- 0.17, where any local-realist theory is capped at S <= 2.
External degrees of freedom — where a particle is and where it's headed — are now confirmed nonlocal too.
The authors note this opens a route to probing where quantum mechanics meets gravity, which couples to motion and mass.
content_html: Bell's theorem is the sharpest knife in quantum foundations: it turns a philosophical dispute about whether particles have definite properties before measurement into an inequality you can test in a lab. That test has now been run on something new — not the polarization of light, not the spin of an atom, but the motion of massive particles.
extra_html: Athreya, Kannan, Yan, Kheruntsyan, Truscott, and Hodgman used pairs of metastable helium atoms whose momenta are entangled, manipulating them with matter-wave interferometry so that a "measurement setting" corresponds to a choice about how the atomic wave packets are recombined. They measure a Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Bell parameter of S = 2.52 +/- 0.17, comfortably above the local-realist ceiling of S = 2. Bell violations with photons and with the internal states of atoms have been standard for decades; extending the result to external degrees of freedom closes a long-standing gap in quantum atom optics. The authors argue the most interesting consequence is what it enables next: gravity couples to mass and to motion, so nonlocal matter waves are a natural place to look for the interplay between quantum mechanics and gravitation.

related.title: Closing the Last Loophole in a Fiber-Based Bell Test
related.hook: Time-bin entanglement is how quantum signals travel down real optical fiber — but the standard measurement quietly throws away photons. This test finally plugs that hole.

related.title: Quantum Entanglement
related.hook: Two particles can share one quantum state so tightly that measuring one instantly fixes the other's matching property — even light-years apart. Einstein called it spooky.

related.title: What Makes Quantum Physics Weird
related.hook: In the quantum world energy comes in lumps, particles act like waves, and you can't pin down everything at once — and yet it's our best-tested theory.

related.title: The Fifth State of Matter, Made in Space
related.hook: Chill a gas to a hair above absolute zero and its atoms stop acting like a crowd and merge into one quantum entity. In orbit, weightlessness lets that strange state last even longer.

flashcards.prompt: What was new about this Bell test compared to earlier ones?
flashcards.back_html: It used the motional (external) states of massive particles — the momenta of entangled helium atoms — rather than photons or internal states like spin.

flashcards.prompt: What does a measured CHSH parameter of S = 2.52 tell you?

choices.text: No local-realist theory can explain the correlations, since such theories cap S at 2
The atoms were measured 2.52 times more accurately than usual
Quantum mechanics predicts S = 2.52 exactly for all systems

flashcards.explanation_html: The CHSH inequality bounds any local hidden-variable theory at S <= 2. Measuring 2.52 +/- 0.17 is a violation well outside the uncertainty.

flashcards.prompt: Why is doing a Bell test with motion, not spin, interesting for gravity?
flashcards.back_html: Gravity couples to mass and motion. Demonstrating nonlocality in the external degrees of freedom of massive particles opens a regime where quantum weirdness and gravity can be probed together.
